title: Voltaire, Wollstonecraft and the Enlightenment's Expanding Circle
subtitle: Who counts? How Enlightenment thinkers widened the circle of moral concern, and where they stopped
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain Voltaire's campaign for religious toleration, including the Calas affair
Describe the aims and significance of Diderot's Encyclopédie
Explain Adam Smith's theory of sympathy and the impartial spectator, and how it relates to Hume
Reconstruct Mary Wollstonecraft's argument in A Vindication of the Rights of Woman and her critique of Rousseau
Use the idea of an 'expanding circle' to assess both the achievements and the blind spots of the Enlightenment
hook:
In October 1761, in the southern French city of Toulouse, a young man named Marc-Antoine Calas was found dead in his family's shop. His family were Protestants in a fiercely Catholic city. A rumour spread that his father, Jean Calas, had killed him to stop him converting to Catholicism. There was no real evidence. Jean Calas, aged sixty-three, was tortured and, in March 1762, executed by being broken on the wheel. He protested his innocence to the end.

Far away, on an estate near the Swiss border, an ageing writer heard the story and could not let it go. He investigated, wrote pamphlets, organised lawyers and lobbied the powerful across Europe. In 1765 the royal court in Paris formally declared Jean Calas innocent. The writer was Voltaire, and his campaign became a symbol of what the Enlightenment hoped reason could do: expose cruelty, defeat fanaticism and widen the circle of people whose suffering counts. Today we meet four thinkers who pushed that circle outwards, and we ask where each of them stopped.

sections.heading: Voltaire: Wit as a Weapon
sections.body:
François-Marie Arouet (1694–1778), who took the pen name **Voltaire** around 1718, was the most famous writer of the eighteenth century. Witty, combative and vain, he wrote plays, poems, histories, philosophical tales and an estimated twenty thousand letters. He was imprisoned in the Bastille twice as a young man, first for satirical verses and then after a quarrel with a nobleman, and after the second time he was allowed to go into exile in England (1726–28).

England transformed him. In his *Letters Concerning the English Nation* (1733, in French as the *Lettres philosophiques*, 1734) he praised English liberty, Newton's science and Locke's philosophy (Days 47 and 52) as models for France. In a famous passage he describes the London Royal Exchange, where Jews, Muslims and Christians do business together as if they were all of the same religion, and the only people they call infidels are those who go bankrupt. If England had only one religion, he observed, there would be danger of tyranny; with two, they would cut each other's throats; but with thirty, they live in peace and happiness. The book was condemned and burned in Paris.

Voltaire was a **deist**: he believed in a creator God, knowable by reason from the order of nature, but rejected revelation, miracles and the authority of churches. He famously wrote that if God did not exist, it would be necessary to invent him, meaning that belief in a God who rewards and punishes is useful for social order. You met his novel *Candide* (1759) on Day 46, his merciless satire of Leibniz's best of all possible worlds.

His enemy was what he called *l'infâme*, the infamous thing, and he signed many letters with the battle cry *Écrasez l'infâme*: crush the infamous thing. By this he meant not religion as such but superstition, fanaticism and the persecuting power of the established Church.

sections.heading: Toleration: The Calas Affair and Beyond
sections.body:
The Calas case gave Voltaire's campaign a human face. In his *Treatise on Toleration* (1763) he argued that persecution is irrational, cruel and contrary to the spirit of religion itself. His arguments are practical and humane. Religious disagreement is inevitable among fallible creatures. Persecution has caused endless suffering and never produced real unity. Countries that tolerate many sects, like England and the Netherlands, are peaceful and prosperous. And all humans are brothers, children of the same Father, who should bear with one another's errors.

Compare Locke's *Letter Concerning Toleration* from Day 52. Locke argued mainly from the nature of belief and the proper limits of government. Voltaire argued from outrage, irony and the evidence of history, and he aimed at a broad public rather than at scholars. Voltaire also fought other cases, including that of the young chevalier de La Barre, executed in 1766 partly for allegedly failing to remove his hat as a religious procession passed, and partly for possessing banned books, among them Voltaire's own *Philosophical Dictionary*.

Two cautions. First, the most famous sentence attributed to Voltaire, I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it, is not his. It was written in 1906 by his English biographer Evelyn Beatrice Hall as a summary of his attitude. Second, Voltaire's own tolerance had sharp limits. His writings contain repeated hostile and contemptuous passages about Jews, and he supported a theory that different human races had separate origins. Historians debate how much these views were central to his thought, but they show that a champion of toleration could still draw the circle narrowly.

sections.heading: Diderot and the Encyclopédie
sections.body:
If Voltaire was the Enlightenment's voice, **Denis Diderot** (1713–1784) was its great organiser. With the mathematician Jean le Rond d'Alembert as co-editor for the early volumes, Diderot directed the *Encyclopédie, or Systematic Dictionary of the Sciences, Arts and Crafts*, published between 1751 and 1772 in seventeen volumes of text and eleven of plates. It eventually contained more than seventy thousand articles by well over a hundred contributors, among them Voltaire, Rousseau (on music) and many specialists.

The *Encyclopédie* was revolutionary in several ways. It treated the **mechanical arts**, the trades and crafts of ordinary working people, as worthy of serious knowledge alongside theology and philosophy. Its magnificent plates show how to make pins, paper, glass and cloth in loving technical detail. It organised knowledge by human faculties (memory, reason, imagination), following Bacon (Day 41), rather than by theological hierarchy. And its cross-references were sometimes used to smuggle in criticism: an orthodox article on a religious topic might point the reader to another article that undermined it.

Diderot wrote in the article 'Encyclopédie' that the aim was not only to gather knowledge but to change the common way of thinking. The authorities understood. The project's official permission was revoked in 1759, and the work had to continue semi-secretly. Diderot later discovered that his own publisher had quietly censored the final volumes behind his back. Earlier, in 1749, Diderot had been imprisoned at Vincennes for his *Letter on the Blind*, which hinted at atheism: the very imprisonment that sent Rousseau walking down that road (Day 53).

The *Encyclopédie* expanded the circle in its own way: it treated knowledge as something that belongs to everyone, including the artisan, and should be shared rather than guarded by priests and professors.

sections.heading: Adam Smith: Sympathy and the Impartial Spectator
sections.body:
Most people know **Adam Smith** (1723–1790) as the author of *The Wealth of Nations* (1776) and the father of modern economics. Fewer know that Smith thought of himself first as a moral philosopher, and that his first book, *The Theory of Moral Sentiments* (1759), was a major work of ethics. Smith was a close friend of Hume (Days 49–50), and his ethics develops Hume's idea that morality rests on sentiment rather than pure reason.

The book's first sentence sets the tone: however selfish man may be supposed, there are evidently some principles in his nature which interest him in the fortune of others, and render their happiness necessary to him, though he derives nothing from it except the pleasure of seeing it. The key principle is **sympathy**, which Smith uses more broadly than we do: our capacity to imagine ourselves in another person's situation and feel something of what they feel. When we see someone about to be struck on the arm, we flinch.

How do we judge our own conduct? Smith's answer is the **impartial spectator**. We learn, through living with others, to look at ourselves as an informed and fair-minded outsider would. Over time we internalise this figure, the man within the breast, which becomes our conscience.

Smith saw clearly that sympathy weakens with distance. In a famous thought experiment he imagines a humane European hearing that a great earthquake has swallowed up the whole empire of China. He would express sorrow, reflect on the precariousness of life, and then go about his business and sleep soundly. Yet if he were to lose his little finger tomorrow, he would not sleep tonight. Does this mean he would sacrifice a hundred million lives to save his finger? Human nature, Smith says, startles with horror at the thought. What stops us is not our feeble sympathy but conscience, the impartial spectator, which shows us that we are but one of the multitude, in no respect better than any other.

Smith's lesson for the expanding circle is double: our natural feelings are partial and local, but reflection can teach us to see ourselves as one among many and to extend our concern.

sections.heading: Mary Wollstonecraft: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
sections.body:
**Mary Wollstonecraft** (1759–1797) grew up in a household troubled by money problems and a violent, drinking father, received little formal education and had to support herself as a lady's companion, a schoolmistress, a governess and finally a writer and translator in London, an unusual career for a woman of her time. In 1790 she published *A Vindication of the Rights of Men*, one of the first replies to Edmund Burke's attack on the French Revolution.

Two years later came her masterpiece, *A Vindication of the Rights of Woman* (1792). Her central argument applies the Enlightenment's own principles with relentless consistency:

1. What gives human beings dignity and rights is reason, the capacity for virtue and knowledge.
2. Women possess reason just as men do.
3. Therefore women deserve the same rights and, above all, the same education.

If women often appear frivolous, vain and weak, Wollstonecraft argues, that is not their nature but the result of an education designed to make them so: trained from childhood to please men, to value beauty over understanding, and to depend on marriage for their survival. Virtue requires independence; a being who is never allowed to think for herself cannot be truly good. Wollstonecraft also argued that this system degraded men and marriage, and that educated, independent women would make better citizens, wives and mothers.

Her sharpest target was Rousseau's *Emile* (Day 53), with its claim that Sophie should be educated to please and serve her husband. Wollstonecraft admired Rousseau's genius but found this view of women contemptible. Against those who feared that educated women would dominate men, she wrote: I do not wish them to have power over men; but over themselves.

She dedicated the book to the French statesman Talleyrand, urging the revolutionaries to include women in their reforms of education. Across the Channel, Olympe de Gouges had published a *Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen* (1791); she was guillotined in 1793. Wollstonecraft herself went to Paris in 1792, witnessed the Revolution, and later married the philosopher William Godwin. She died in 1797, aged thirty-eight, from an infection after giving birth to her second daughter, Mary, who would grow up to write *Frankenstein*. Godwin's frank memoir of her unconventional life in 1798 scandalised readers, and her reputation suffered for a century before later feminists reclaimed her.

sections.heading: The Expanding Circle and Its Edges
sections.body:
Step back and the shared pattern is clear. Each of today's thinkers took a principle that their society professed, reason, humanity, sympathy, the rights of man, and asked whether it was being applied consistently. Voltaire asked why Protestants should be tortured by people who claimed to follow a merciful God. Diderot asked why the knowledge of artisans should count for less than the knowledge of theologians. Smith asked why a distant earthquake should matter less than one's own finger. Wollstonecraft asked why the rights of man should stop at women.

This method, holding a society to its own ideals, would become one of the most powerful engines of moral change. In the same years, the formerly enslaved writer Olaudah Equiano published his *Interesting Narrative* (1789), and the campaign against the slave trade grew in Britain. Its arguments drew on Christian conscience as well as Enlightenment ideas of natural rights and common humanity.

Yet every thinker in this lesson also drew the circle somewhere. Voltaire's contempt for Jews, Locke's exclusion of atheists and Catholics (Day 52), Rousseau's subordination of women, Hume's racist footnote (Day 50) and Kant's racial hierarchies (Day 57) show how deeply the prejudices of the age persisted among its most brilliant critics. Even Wollstonecraft wrote mainly for middle-class women and said little about the poor or the enslaved, though she condemned slavery.

How should we judge them? One response dismisses the Enlightenment's universalism as a mask for European power. Another, which many historians defend, notes that the Enlightenment's own principles supplied the arguments that later exposed its blind spots: Wollstonecraft against Rousseau, abolitionists against slaveholders, and many later voices you will meet on Day 86. The expanding circle was not a finished achievement but an unfinished project, and it is still being argued over today.

keyQuote.text: I do not wish them to have power over men; but over themselves.
keyQuote.source: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792), Chapter 4

modernConnection.title: How Far Should Our Circle Reach?
modernConnection.body:
In 1981 the philosopher Peter Singer published *The Expanding Circle*, arguing that moral progress consists largely in extending concern from family and tribe to nation, to all of humanity and finally to all beings capable of suffering. He borrowed the image from the nineteenth-century historian W. E. H. Lecky, but the method is today's lesson: take the reasons that make suffering matter, and apply them consistently. You will meet Singer's drowning child and his case for animals on Day 83.

Adam Smith's earthquake in China is now an everyday experience. Your phone brings you images of floods, famines and wars in real time. Smith predicted what research on 'compassion fatigue' and the 'identifiable victim effect' has since documented: we respond more strongly to one named, photographed person than to statistics about thousands, and attention fades quickly. The photograph of the drowned toddler Alan Kurdi in 2015 briefly transformed European debates about refugees in a way that years of figures had not. Charities know this, which is why fundraising appeals feature one face rather than a chart. Smith's hope was that reflection, not just feeling, could close the gap.

The circle is still being argued over. Should it include animals? Future generations (Day 88)? Ecosystems? Perhaps one day artificial minds (Day 89)? Each debate repeats the Enlightenment move: identify what makes a being matter, then ask whether we are applying it consistently.

But the image of a steadily expanding circle can mislead. Moral concern can also contract, as it did in the twentieth century's genocides, when whole groups were deliberately pushed outside it. Extending concern to distant strangers can collide with special obligations to family and community, which care ethicists defend (Day 85). And, as Wollstonecraft knew, it is not enough to feel sympathy for those outside the circle: they must be recognised as equals who can speak and act for themselves.

vocabulary.definition: Allowing beliefs and practices one disapproves of, rather than suppressing them by force; Voltaire's central cause.
vocabulary.example: Voltaire's campaign for Jean Calas made toleration a matter of public outrage, not just theory.

vocabulary.definition: Belief in a creator God knowable through reason and the order of nature, combined with rejection of revelation, miracles and church authority.
vocabulary.example: Voltaire's deism let him attack the Church while still believing in a divine architect.

vocabulary.definition: 'Crush the infamous thing': Voltaire's slogan against superstition, fanaticism and religious persecution.
vocabulary.example: Voltaire signed letters to friends with Écrasez l'infâme as a rallying cry.

vocabulary.definition: The great French reference work edited by Diderot and d'Alembert (1751–1772), aiming to gather all knowledge, including the crafts, and to change the common way of thinking.
vocabulary.example: The Encyclopédie's plates showing glassmaking treated artisans' knowledge as worthy of study.

vocabulary.definition: For Adam Smith, the capacity to imagine ourselves in another's situation and share something of their feelings; the basis of moral judgement.
vocabulary.example: Flinching when you see someone about to be hit is sympathy in Smith's sense.

vocabulary.definition: Smith's imagined fair-minded observer whose judgement we internalise as conscience when evaluating our own conduct.
vocabulary.example: Before sending an angry email, she asked how an impartial spectator would view it.

vocabulary.definition: The idea that moral progress consists in extending moral concern to ever wider groups of beings.
vocabulary.example: The abolition of slavery and the extension of votes to women are often cited as stages of the expanding circle.

vocabulary.definition: The view that certain rights, values or moral principles apply equally to all human beings, regardless of sex, religion, nation or race.
vocabulary.example: Wollstonecraft used Enlightenment universalism to argue that the rights of man must include women.

thinkingExercise.title: Draw Your Own Circle
thinkingExercise.prompt: Every thinker in this lesson drew the circle of moral concern somewhere. Spend 10–15 minutes mapping your own.
steps: Draw a set of concentric circles on paper. Put yourself in the centre, then place, from inside out: family, friends, fellow citizens, people in distant countries, future generations, animals, and anything else you think belongs.
For each ring, write one sentence explaining what makes these beings matter morally to you (reason, ability to suffer, relationship, shared citizenship).
Apply the Enlightenment test: is your reason applied consistently? If suffering matters for distant humans, why not animals? If relationship matters for family, why help strangers at all?
Recall Smith's earthquake. Name one distant tragedy you heard about recently and honestly rate how much it affected you compared with a minor problem of your own.
Finally, imagine a reader in 2200 looking back at you. Which of your current beliefs about who counts do you think they might find as shocking as we find Voltaire's or Rousseau's blind spots?

summary: Voltaire used wit and public campaigns, most famously in the Calas affair and his Treatise on Toleration (1763), to fight fanaticism and persecution, though his own writings contain antisemitic passages.
Diderot's Encyclopédie (1751–1772) aimed to gather all knowledge, including the crafts of ordinary workers, and to change the common way of thinking, despite repeated suppression.
Adam Smith's Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759) grounded morality in sympathy and the impartial spectator, recognising that sympathy weakens with distance but conscience can correct it.
Mary Wollstonecraft's Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) argued that women share reason and so deserve equal rights and education, and attacked Rousseau's ideal of the subservient Sophie.
The Enlightenment expanded the circle of moral concern by holding society to its own principles, yet each thinker left some people outside; those same principles later exposed the gaps.

quiz.question: What was the Calas affair?
options: A dispute between Voltaire and Rousseau over music
The banning of the Encyclopédie
The torture and execution of a Protestant father falsely accused of killing his son, which Voltaire campaigned to overturn
Voltaire's imprisonment in the Bastille
quiz.explanation: Jean Calas was executed in Toulouse in 1762; Voltaire's campaign helped win his posthumous exoneration in 1765.

quiz.question: Who actually wrote the line 'I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it'?
options: Evelyn Beatrice Hall, Voltaire's biographer, in 1906
Voltaire, in the Treatise on Toleration
Voltaire, in Candide
John Locke, in A Letter Concerning Toleration
quiz.explanation: Hall coined it as a summary of Voltaire's attitude. It does not appear in his writings.

quiz.question: What did Voltaire mean by l'infâme?
options: The French monarchy
Superstition, fanaticism and the persecuting power of the established Church
Leibniz's philosophy
The English Parliament
quiz.explanation: Voltaire was a deist, not an atheist; his target was religious fanaticism and persecution rather than belief in God.

quiz.question: Which feature made Diderot's Encyclopédie especially radical?
options: It was written entirely by Diderot himself
It was sponsored and approved by the Catholic Church
It argued that knowledge should be kept for experts
It treated the trades and crafts of ordinary workers as serious knowledge and used cross-references to slip in criticism
quiz.explanation: The Encyclopédie elevated the mechanical arts and aimed to change the common way of thinking, which is why it was repeatedly suppressed.

quiz.question: In Smith's earthquake thought experiment, what stops a person from being willing to sacrifice millions of distant lives to save his little finger?
options: His strong natural sympathy for the distant victims
Fear of legal punishment
Conscience, the impartial spectator, which shows him he is only one among many
A calculation of economic self-interest
quiz.explanation: Smith admits that our sympathy for distant people is weak; it is the internalised impartial spectator that corrects our partiality.

quiz.question: What was the core argument of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman?
options: Women share in reason, so they deserve equal rights and education; their apparent weaknesses are the product of a bad education
Women are naturally superior to men and should govern
Women should be educated mainly to be pleasing companions for men
Rights belong only to property owners
quiz.explanation: Wollstonecraft argued from the Enlightenment premise that reason grounds rights; the third option is the view of Rousseau that she attacked.

quiz.question: A charity raises far more money with a photograph of one hungry child than with statistics about a million. Which idea from today's lesson does this best illustrate?
options: Voltaire's deism
The mechanical arts
Écrasez l'infâme
Smith's observation that sympathy is strongest for what is near and vivid, and weak for the distant and abstract
quiz.explanation: Smith saw that our natural sympathy is partial; modern psychology calls this pattern the identifiable victim effect.

quiz.question: Adam Smith's Theory of Moral Sentiments was published before The Wealth of Nations.
quiz.explanation: The Theory of Moral Sentiments appeared in 1759, seventeen years before The Wealth of Nations (1776).

quiz.question: Wollstonecraft admired Rousseau's plan for Sophie's education in Emile and recommended it for all girls.
quiz.explanation: She attacked it: educating girls only to please men, she argued, made them dependent and prevented real virtue.

quiz.question: Voltaire was an atheist who believed belief in God was harmful to society.
quiz.explanation: Voltaire was a deist and even wrote that if God did not exist, it would be necessary to invent him.

goDeeper.body:
Historians have fiercely debated what kind of movement the Enlightenment was, and whose it was.

Jonathan Israel, in a multi-volume history beginning with *Radical Enlightenment* (2001), argues that there were really two Enlightenments. A **moderate Enlightenment**, represented by Locke, Voltaire and most of the famous names, sought to reconcile reason with religion, monarchy and existing social hierarchies. A **radical Enlightenment**, rooted in Spinoza (Day 45) and carried forward by Diderot and others, pressed on to democracy, full equality, freedom of the press and the separation of morality from theology. On Israel's account, it was the radical stream that produced modern democratic values. Critics reply that he exaggerates Spinoza's influence and makes the story too tidy.

Another debate concerns the Enlightenment's attitude to empire and race. Some scholars, building on Max Horkheimer and Theodor Adorno's *Dialectic of Enlightenment* (1944, Day 80), argue that its universal reason became a tool of domination. Others, such as Sankar Muthu in *Enlightenment Against Empire* (2003), show that Diderot, Kant and Herder wrote powerful critiques of European colonialism. Diderot's contributions to the abbé Raynal's *History of the Two Indies* contain passionate denunciations of slavery and conquest.

Finally, Wollstonecraft's place in philosophy has been re-evaluated. Long treated as a pamphleteer, she is now read as a serious moral and political philosopher whose idea that virtue requires independence connects to republican theories of freedom as non-domination, defended today by Philip Pettit. On that view, a person is unfree not only when someone interferes with her, but whenever she lives at another's mercy, as Wollstonecraft argued married women did.

questions: Is it fair to judge eighteenth-century thinkers by today's moral standards? What would be lost if we refused to judge them at all?
Smith thought conscience could correct the partiality of sympathy. Is that true in your experience, or do we mostly stay partial?
Which group, if any, do you think is still outside the circle of moral concern today, and what argument would bring them in?
